| [LIT-097](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-097.md) v3 | The Extended Mind | Clark & Chalmers (1998), DOI-10.1093/analys/58.1.7. The four "criteria" for a coupled resource (constancy, direct availability, automatic endorsement, and the admittedly "arguable" past conscious endorsement) are offered as the features that make the paradigm case clear. | [LIT-130](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-130.md) v2 | Personal Identity and Ethics | Dufner (2025), <https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/identity-ethics/>. A survey, arguing no thesis of its own, of how three contested questions bear on ethics: which account of persistence is true (unique psychological continuity, Shoemaker and Parfit; or biological continuity and animalism, Olson and DeGrazia), whether identity or the psychological relations (continuity and/or connectedness) is what matters (Parfit's fission case), and whether metaphysics constrains ethics or the reverse. It traces these through prudential concern, responsibility, abortion (Marquis), death and brain-death criteria, dementia and advance directives (Dworkin vs Jaworska on Margo), and the separateness of persons (Rawls, Parfit, Nozick, Taurek, Sidgwick, Brink). Its main recurring finding is that the relation that fixes persistence and the relation that matters ethically keep coming apart. It concludes that all three questions remain open. | Active — read in full 2026-09-26 ([NOTE-166](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-166.md)); worth reading as the current, compact reference map from theories of persistence to applied ethics; it is a survey that takes no side, so it is a route to the primary sources (Parfit 1984, Olson 1997, McMahan 2002, Schechtman 1996, Korsgaard 1989) rather than a source of claims. |

| [LIT-292](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-292.md) v2 | Identification and Identity | Velleman (2002), DOI-10.7551/mitpress/2143.003.0007. Velleman targets Frankfurt's *later* conception of autonomy. On that conception, a person acts autonomously only when his volitions derive from "the essential character of his will", and that essence consists of volitional necessities that are also the conditions of his personal identity. Velleman argues against it on three grounds. Such an essence would ground authenticity, not autonomy (the Winnicottian False Self is inauthentic but over-controlled). Frankfurt offers no argument or example that motivational change ends a person. And the ideal of wholeheartedness, which cures ambivalence by extruding a desire from the self, is a defensive fantasy: Freud's Rat Man was made ill by just such a separation, and identifying with part of oneself in the ordinary, imaginative sense is Sartrean bad faith. He replaces "the self" with an *aspectual* reading of "self" as a marker of reflexivity. On that reading autonomy is behaviour motivated partly by the understanding, the part of us "with which we cannot help identifying", without its being our identity (pp. 357–360). | Active — read in full 2026-09-29 ([NOTE-268](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-268.md)); worth reading as the sharpest critique of Frankfurt's late (1990s) identification of autonomy with a volitional essence, and as a careful source for what Frankfurt said in the essays collected in *Necessity, Volition, and Love* (1999). It is not a survey of the 1971–1987 hierarchical account, which it summarizes in one paragraph and defers to "What Happens When Someone Acts?"; its positive view is stated "briefly" and explicitly deferred to other essays. |

| [LIT-432](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-432.md) | The Emotion Machine: Commonsense Thinking, Artificial Intelligence, and the Future of the Human Mind | Minsky (2006), Simon & Schuster, read in the author's 2005 draft. | [LIT-446](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-446.md) | Survival and Identity | Lewis (1976), DOI-10.1525/9780520353060-002. What matters in survival is mental continuity and connectedness (the R-relation among person-stages), and it is also identity, because the two answers relate different things. Against Perry: two persons, not three, took part in a fission. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-373](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-373.md)), from a scan of the 1976 printing posted on Andrew M. It agrees with Parfit that what matters is mental continuity and connectedness, the R-relation among person-stages, and denies that this conflicts with identity: persons are maximal R-interrelated aggregates of stages, so the relation of being stages of one person is the R-relation. Fission becomes two persons sharing their early stages, and degrees are handled by supervaluation. A reconciliation by redefinition of counting, which Lewis grants is "somewhat counterintuitive". |

| [LIT-451](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-451.md) | Of Personal Identity | Hume (1739), Treatise 1.4.6, with the Appendix (1740). There is no impression of a self, "constant and invariable", so no idea of one: introspection finds only "some particular perception or other", and the mind is "a bundle or collection of different perceptions". The identity we ascribe to it is "fictitious", like that of plants, ships and churches: an easy transition of the imagination along resemblance and causation, with memory discovering rather than producing it, so that hard cases are "grammatical" rather than philosophical. The Appendix retracts the account of the connecting principle: two principles he cannot reconcile or renounce leave the matter "too hard for my understanding". | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-386](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-386.md)), in the Merivale–Millican critical text on davidhume.org, with the Appendix's second thoughts (App. 10–21); worth reading as the founding statement of the bundle view and the first published retraction of it. The section finds no impression of a self, calls the mind "a bundle or collection of different perceptions", and explains our ascription of identity to it as a fiction of the imagination run on resemblance and causation, the same fiction that makes a repaired ship or a rebuilt church "the same". The Appendix then confesses that it cannot explain what unites the perceptions and leaves the problem "too hard for my understanding". The section's case is introspective and associationist; its Appendix is the clearest statement of what any bundle view owes. |
| [LIT-452](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-452.md) | Against Narrativity | Strawson (2004), Ratio 17(4):428–452. Rejects both the psychological Narrativity thesis (people do experience their lives as a story) and the ethical one (they should, to be full persons), naming Sacks, Bruner, Dennett, Taylor, MacIntyre and Schechtman. Distinguishes Diachronic self-experience (the self I am now was there in the past) from Episodic (it was not, though the human being was), and splits Narrativity into form-finding, story-telling and revision, with only story-telling sufficient. Episodics are normal and can live well; self-narration risks falsifying the self it describes. | [LIT-453](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-453.md) | Philosophical conceptions of the self: implications for cognitive science | Gallagher (2000), Trends in Cognitive Sciences 4(1):14–21. Divides philosophical accounts of the self into the "minimal self", accessible to present self-consciousness without temporal extension, and the "narrative self", extended in time through memory and story. Neonatal imitation suggests an embodied minimal self; Strawson's and Tani's are momentary. Against Dennett's narrative centre, the self is "the sum total of its narratives". | [LIT-454](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-454.md) | Personal Identity | Olson (2002, rev. 2023), Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. Separates seven questions (characterization, personhood, persistence, evidence, population, personal ontology, what matters) and then takes up persistence. Three answers: psychological continuity (the majority view, repaired from Locke's memory criterion via causal dependence), brute-physical continuity (animalism), and anticriterialism. Fission forces the psychological view into multiple occupancy or a non-branching clause, which makes identity not what matters. The too-many-thinkers objection says that if we are not our animals there are two thinkers in every chair. Temporal-parts ontology may leave it indeterminate what we are. Avoids the word "self". | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-374](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-374.md)); worth reading as the standard map of the analytic personal-identity debate, written by the leading animalist. It separates seven questions that are usually run together, then works the persistence question through psychological-continuity, brute-physical and anticriterialist answers, fission and the too-many-thinkers objection. It is a survey with a side: §§6–7 put the case for animalism more fully than the case against it, and the entry sets the word "self" aside, so the narrative and minimal selves are outside it. |
| [LIT-460](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-460.md) | Role play with large language models | Shanahan, McDonell & Reynolds (2023), Nature 623:493–498. A dialogue agent is an LLM role-playing the character its prompt describes, or more exactly a simulator keeping a superposition of simulacra consistent with the conversation. Only simulacra can appear to have beliefs, goals or a self; the simulator has none, "not even simulated versions", and "it is role play all the way down". When an agent says it wants to survive there is "no-one at home". Each role-played character would carry its own theory of selfhood, which the conversation narrows; what an agent would try to preserve (hardware, process, instance) is left open. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-370](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-370.md)), in the Nature text with the arXiv v1 preprint compared; worth reading here as the source of the simulator/simulacra account that every LLM-selfhood paper in this record answers. On it nothing is a self: the simulator has no beliefs, goals or agency "of its own, not even simulated versions", and a simulacrum only role-plays a character that has them ("no-one at home"). Its one section on selfhood asks which self a role-played character would try to preserve, not what the system is, and leaves identity over time for a dialogue agent "far from clear". The denial of a self is asserted from the framing, not argued against a rival. |
| [LIT-462](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-462.md) | The Self and the Future | Williams (1970), DOI-10.2307/2183946. One experiment, told twice. A and B enter a machine that exchanges their memories and characters, and choose selfishly which emerging person gets $100,000 and which torture: the outcomes make "changing bodies" the natural description. Told as a series of things that will happen to me (amnesia, changed character, another's "memories", then torture), fear stays rational at every step, and the step that completes the swap changes only what happens to someone else. Undecidability and convention make the clash worse, not better. If forced to choose selfishly, pass the pain to the other body, and call it a "risk". | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-387](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-387.md)), in a JSTOR copy of the published article posted on a University of Vermont course page; worth reading as the strongest case that first-person concern tracks the body, and the paper that made the reduplication-free body swap a problem for the psychological view. It tells one body-exchange experiment twice. Told third-personally, with choices before and reactions after, it says A and B swap bodies. Told first-personally, as a series of things that will happen to me before I am tortured, it says I am the one tortured. It argues that neither indeterminacy nor convention can resolve the clash, and ends with a "rather shaky" preference for the bodily answer, as a "risk". An argument from what fear is rational, not a theory. |
| [LIT-463](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-463.md) | Subjectivity and Selfhood: Investigating the First-Person Perspective | Zahavi (2005), MIT Press. Per its publisher, a defence of the self against neuroscientists and philosophers who doubt it, arguing that "the notion of self is crucial for a proper understanding of consciousness" and that experience, self-awareness and selfhood cannot be understood apart. It uses Husserl, Heidegger, Sartre and Merleau-Ponty to give an account of the "experiential givenness of the self" for philosophy of mind, cognitive science, developmental psychology and psychiatry. Its chapters run from self-awareness and phenomenal consciousness through time-consciousness and reflection to self and other, theory of mind, autism and embodiment. Unread: registered from the description and the contents. | Deferred — registered 2026-10-02 from the publisher's description and the chapter list on Crossref, not read: no lawful full text could be reached. The MIT Press Direct edition is not open access (Crossref carries no licence, OpenAlex reports it closed), and no author copy of the book is posted. It stays Deferred until a copy is supplied, not on merit. |
| [LIT-464](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-464.md) | Of Identity and Diversity | Locke (1694), Essay II.xxvii, added in the second edition. Identity is relative to the idea the name stands for: the same mass is the same particles, the same oak or horse or man is the same continued life, and the same person is the same consciousness. A person is "a thinking intelligent being" that "can consider itself as itself", and personal identity reaches "as far as this consciousness can be extended backwards to any past action or thought". It is independent of substance, material or immaterial: the prince's consciousness in the cobbler's body is the same person but not the same man. "Person" is "a forensic term", grounding reward and punishment. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-385](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-385.md)), in the Wikisource transcription of the 1853 Troutman & Hayes reprint of the sixth-edition text, compared word by word with Project Gutenberg's; worth reading as the founding text of the psychological account of personal identity and the source of the record's whole line on what a person is. It separates the same substance, the same man and the same person, puts the person in "consciousness" extended back to past actions, and calls "person" a "forensic term". Its cases, the prince and the cobbler, the day-man and the night-man, the severed little finger, are argued from intuition, and its key relation, "the same consciousness", is never defined. |
| [LIT-465](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-465.md) | Simulacra as Conscious Exotica | Shanahan (2024), Inquiry 69(6):2982–3010, from arXiv:2402.12422. After Wittgenstein, consciousness words mean only what is public, so the question for an exotic entity is whether we could "engineer an encounter" with it in a shared world and what a society-wide conversation would then say. Disembodied chat agents are not even candidates; virtually embodied LLM agents could be. Tool use and memory make belief talk increasingly literal, but a chat agent has no "self worth preserving", and a role player has no "person behind the mask": its identity is a shifting distribution of roles. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-382](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-382.md)) in the arXiv v2 preprint (July 2024), not the Inquiry version of record, which returned 403; worth reading as the Wittgensteinian alternative to the evidential debate about AI consciousness. It replaces "is it conscious?" with "could we engineer an encounter with it, and how would our language adapt?", and so counts disembodied chat agents as not even candidates. On the self it is brief and pointed: a chat agent has "nothing that would qualify as a self worth preserving", lacking body, personal history and autobiographical memory, and a role-playing agent has no "person behind the mask"; its identity, "insofar as that notion even made sense", is the shifting distribution of roles. It argues by method and scenario, not evidence, and says so. |
| [LIT-466](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-466.md) | Palatable Conceptions of Disembodied Being | Shanahan (2025), arXiv:2503.16348. Asks whether consciousness talk can be stretched to disembodied, 2024-vintage LLM agents. Their time would be discrete and discontinuous, a string of unlike beads. Their "I" has two palatable referents, the model across conversations and a self confined to one conversation that "flickers into being with each user interaction", and we may slip between them. Such selves can be edited, copied and merged, and smeared across branching simulacra. Every candidate site dissolves, which Shanahan reads as Buddhist emptiness, and turns back on human selfhood. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-376](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-376.md)) in arXiv v3 (July 2025), the only text there is; worth reading as the one paper here that argues directly about what an LLM's self is, rather than whether it has one. Its answer: two conceptions are in play, a self sited in the model and "fleeting, flickering" selves sited in single conversations, and we may slip between them; every candidate site "dissolves upon close examination", and Shanahan takes that to the Buddhist conclusion that there is no inherent self, here or in us. It is avowedly "poetic", not literal, and its examples are invented usages, not data. |
| [LIT-467](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-467.md) | Being No One: The Self-Model Theory of Subjectivity | Metzinger (2003), MIT Press. Per its publisher, "no such things as selves exist in the world: nobody ever had or was a self. All that exists are phenomenal selves", and the phenomenal self is "the content of a 'transparent self-model'". A representationalist and functional analysis of the conscious first-person perspective, with conceptual "tools", constraints on consciousness and neurophenomenological case studies (agnosia, neglect, blindsight, hallucination), asking whether being someone can be analysed at subpersonal levels. Unread: registered from the description and the contents; the theory is read in [LIT-450](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-450.md). | Deferred — registered 2026-10-02 from the publisher's description and the chapter list on Crossref, not read: no lawful full text of the book could be reached. The MIT Press Direct edition is not open access and no author copy is posted. Its theory is read in Metzinger's own short statement, "Self models" ([LIT-450](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-450.md), read in full). It stays Deferred until a copy is supplied, not on merit. |
| [LIT-468](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-468.md) | The Constitution of Selves | Schechtman (1996), Cornell University Press. Separates the reidentification question (is this the same person?) from the characterization question (which actions, experiences and traits are this person's own?), and argues against analytic philosophy's attention to the first at the expense of the second. Chapters 1–3 take up reidentification; chapters 4–6 give the narrative self-constitution view, on which, as Strawson quotes it, a person "creates his identity [only] by forming an autobiographical narrative". The source of the term "characterization question" in the SEP map. Unread: registered from the description and the contents. | Deferred — registered 2026-10-02 from the publisher's description, the Library of Congress record and the chapter list on Crossref, not read: no lawful full text could be reached. The Cornell/De Gruyter eBook is sold, not open, and the Internet Archive copy is for print-disabled users only. It stays Deferred until a copy is supplied, not on merit. |
| [LIT-469](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-469.md) | Reasons and Persons | Parfit (1984), Clarendon Press; DOI-10.1093/019824908X.001.0001 is the 1986 reprint online. Four loosely connected parts, per the author's abstract: self-defeating theories of rationality and morality; what one person can rationally want at different times, and attitudes to time; personal identity, where "most of us … have certain beliefs about this subject that are false, but hard to give up"; and obligations to future generations, with the non-identity problem and the Repugnant Conclusion. By the chapter abstracts, Part III defends a reductionist view on which identity is not what matters and draws consequences for self-interest and distributive justice. Unread. | Deferred — registered 2026-10-02 from the publisher's description, its chapter abstracts and the table of contents; the book is in copyright and no lawful full text was reachable (the Internet Archive copies are lending-only and were not opened), so it is unread and no NOTE is filed. By its publisher's account, Part III argues that most of us hold false beliefs about personal identity, that psychological continuity and connectedness, not identity, is what matters, and that this should change our attitudes to our own future, to rationality and to morality. The record already leans on it at second hand: Birch's Relation R, Velleman's reading of Frankfurt and the identity-and-ethics survey all cite it. |
| [LIT-491](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-491.md) | Categories We Live By: The Construction of Sex, Gender, Race, and Other Social Categories | Ásta (2018), OUP. Per its publisher, a theory of social categories built on the question "what is it for a feature of an individual to be socially meaningful?"; its main idea is that "social categories are conferred upon people", and its "conferralist" framework is applied to sex, gender, race, disability and other categories, and to their tendency to oppress. Unread: filed from the description and contents only. | Deferred — filed 2026-10-02 from the publisher's description and table of contents; no lawful full text was reachable (the book is not open access, Oxford Academic is paywalled, and the author's site posts replies and related essays but no chapters or drafts), so it is not read and no NOTE is filed. It is the book-length statement of conferralism, the main rival to Haslanger's account of social categories ([LIT-480](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-480.md)); what it argues beyond the description is not recorded here. |
